title: Consider an implementation of an unsorted singly linked list and
subject: Data Structure
text:
Consider an unsorted singly linked list represented with both a head pointer and a tail pointer.

Which of the following operations can be implemented in O(1) time?

  • I. Insertion at the front of the linked list

  • II. Insertion at the end of the linked list

  • III. Deletion of the front node of the linked list

  • IV. Deletion of the last node of the linked list
solution:
Concept

An operation on a linked list is O(1) only when it touches nothing but a pointer the list already tracks -- no search for any other node. A singly linked list carries a forward link only: from any node you can reach the next node, but not the one before it. So the moment an operation needs a node's predecessor, and no pointer already points at that predecessor, finding it costs an O(n) walk from the head.

Application

  1. Insertion at the front (I): link the new node's next pointer to the current head, then move the head pointer to the new node. Both steps use only the head pointer -- O(1).

  2. Insertion at the end (II): link the current tail's next pointer to the new node, then move the tail pointer to the new node. Both steps use only the tail pointer -- O(1).

  3. Deletion of the front node (III): move the head pointer to the head's next node. This uses only the head pointer -- O(1).

  4. Deletion of the last node (IV): the tail pointer must move to the node just before the current tail -- the new last node. But nothing in this list points backward from the tail to that node, so it can only be found by walking from the head until reaching the node whose next is the current tail -- O(n).

Cross-check

This is exactly the gap a doubly linked list closes: there, each node also stores a prev pointer, so tail.prev would name the second-last node directly and its deletion would be O(1) too. The absence of that backward link in a singly linked list is the entire reason IV needs a traversal even though a tail pointer is present.

So operations I, II and III run in O(1) time and IV does not -- the answer is I, II and III.

Each of these needs only a pointer the list already tracks -- the head for the front operations and the tail for the end insertion -- moved once, with no other node to search for; that is what keeps every one of them at O(1).

The fast pointer travels two nodes per step, while the slow pointer only moves one. The slow pointer will point to the middle node of the linked list when the fast pointer points to the last node, i.e. when the next node is null.

title: Consider the following code: struct node int data; struct node
subject: Data Structure
text:
Consider the following code:

struct node {
    int data;
    struct node *next;
} *head;

void initialize() {
    head = NULL;
}

void fun1(int num) {
    struct node *Node1 = (struct node *) malloc(sizeof(struct node));
    Node1->data = num;
    Node1->next = head;
    head = Node1;
}

void fun2(struct node *head, int num) {
    if (head == NULL) {
        return;
    }
    struct node *Node2 = (struct node *) malloc(sizeof(struct node));
    Node2->data = num;
    Node2->next = NULL;
    while (head->next != NULL)
        head = head->next;
    head->next = Node2;
}

Choose the statement that is valid about what these function definitions guarantee or permit; do not assume an unstated sequence of calls:

options.html: The code will give a run time error
Code will create a linked list and insert 2 nodes in the linked list.
The code will insert a node in an empty linked list and then it add one more element at the end of the linked list.
The code can add more than 2 elements at the end of the linked list.

solution:
Concept

A function definition describes an operation that can occur when the function is called; defining the function does not execute its body. In C, a pointer argument is passed by value, so advancing the parameter changes only the local pointer copy, while writing through that pointer can still modify the linked nodes.

For a singly linked list, insertion at the tail requires a nonempty starting pointer, traversal to the node whose next link is null, and then assignment of that link to the new node.

Application

  1. The global head has static storage duration and is initially null even before initialize is called.

  2. fun1 allocates one node, links its next field to the current global head, and then updates the global head. This operation can create the first node when it is actually called.

  3. fun2 first returns when its argument is null. Otherwise it allocates one node, advances its local head copy to the current tail, and writes the tail link through next. Advancing the local copy does not alter the global head.

  4. No statement in the snippet calls either insertion function. Therefore the snippet alone does not guarantee that a list or an exact two-node sequence will be created. Its reusable tail-insertion function can, however, be called repeatedly after a nonempty list exists.

Cross-check

  • fun1(10) produces 10 -> NULL when called from the initial state.

  • fun2(head, 20) then produces 10 -> 20 -> NULL; another call such as fun2(head, 30) produces 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> NULL. The global head remains at the first node.

  • The absence of calls explains why the two-node claims are not guaranteed, and pass-by-value explains why traversing the parameter is not a runtime-error mechanism.

Result

The defensible statement is: “The code can add more than 2 elements at the end of the linked list.”

optionFeedback.html: fun2 receives head by value. Assigning head = head->next moves that local pointer copy, while head->next = Node2 writes through the copy to a node link.
Both node allocations are inside the bodies of fun1 and fun2. The snippet presents those function definitions, while a caller supplies whether and how often either body executes.
fun1 supports insertion at the global head. fun2 supports a tail insertion from a non-null supplied head; a caller supplies the invocation order and count.
fun2 supports one tail insertion per non-null invocation. Each invocation starts from the supplied head, reaches the current tail, and links one newly allocated node there.

title: Consider singly linked list of the form Where is pointer
subject: Data Structure
text:
Consider a singly linked list of the form

Where F is a pointer to the first element in the list and L is a pointer to the last element in the list. The time of which of the following operations depends on the length of the list?

options.html: Delete the last element of the list
Delete the first element of the list
Add an element after last element of the list
Interchange the first two elements of the list

solution:
Delete the last element of the list (Option A):

In a singly linked list, to delete the last element, you must traverse the entire list to find the second-to-last node (as there

is no backward pointer).

Time complexity depends on the length of the list.

Correct answer: This operation is affected by the length of the list.

Delete the first element of the list (Option B):

The first element can be removed in constant time by simply updating the F pointer to point to the second element.

Time complexity is O(1).

Add an element after the last element of the list (Option C):

Since L directly points to the last element, adding a new element after it takes constant time.

Time complexity is O(1).

Interchange the first two elements of the list (Option D):

This operation involves swapping the first two elements, which requires constant time.

Time complexity is O(1).

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Deleting the last node in a singly linked list that only has forward pointers requires locating the node just before the last so its next pointer can be set to null and the L pointer updated. That typically requires traversing from F to the second-to-last node, so the time grows with the number of nodes (O(n)). Note: if the list has exactly one node, deletion can be done in O(1) by setting F and L to null.
Deleting the first node takes constant time (O(1)). Simply set F to F.next; if the list becomes empty after removal, also set L to null. No traversal of the list is required.

Adding a new element after the last node is O(1) when you maintain a pointer to the last node (L). Create the new node, set L.next to the new node, and update L to point to the new node. No traversal is needed.

Swapping the first two nodes is a constant-time operation (O(1)). If there are at least two nodes, update the few next pointers to exchange their order; if there are fewer than two nodes, nothing needs to be done. No traversal of the list is required.

title: At hill station, the parking lot is one long driveway
subject: Data Structure
text: At a hill station, the parking lot is one long driveway snaking up a hill side. Car drive in and park right behind the car in front of them, one behind another. A car can’t leave until all the cars in front of it have left. Is the parking lot more like
solution:
Answer: A queue (first-in, first-out).

Explanation: Cars drive in and park one behind another. The car that arrived first is at the front and can leave before the cars that arrived later. No car can pass those in front, so departures happen in the same order as arrivals — first-in, first-out (FIFO).

  • How this maps to a queue: cars form a line; the earliest-arrived car is removed first, matching queue behavior.

  • Why a stack is not appropriate: a stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO), which would require the most recently parked car to leave first — not possible here.

  • Why 'array' or 'linked list' are not the best conceptual match: these describe storage or connection methods but do not specify the enforced FIFO removal policy. A queue is the abstract data structure that captures the required behavior.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. An array describes a way of storing elements in contiguous memory and allows direct access by index. The parking lot enforces an exit order (cars cannot leave until those in front leave), which is a behavioral constraint (first-in, first-out) rather than just a storage layout. While an array could store the sequence of cars, it does not by itself express the FIFO exit rule.

Incorrect. A stack follows last-in, first-out (LIFO): the most recently added item is removed first. In this parking scenario, the most recently parked car cannot leave before the cars parked in front, so LIFO does not match the situation.
Correct. The parking lot enforces first-in, first-out (FIFO): cars line up and the car that arrived first (at the front) is the first that can leave. This behavior is exactly what a queue models.

Incorrect. A linked list is a structure of nodes pointing to the next element; it describes how elements are connected but does not by itself enforce a removal policy. A linked list can be used to implement a queue, but the defining behavior of the parking lot is FIFO (a queue), not merely the underlying storage representation.

title: The following function takes singly linked list as input argument.
subject: Data Structure
text:
The following C function takes a singly linked list as input argument.
int kg(struct node head){
          struct node p1 = head, *p2 = head;
          if(head → next != NULL){
                    p1 = head → next;
                    p2 = (head→next)?head→next→next : NULL;
          }
          while( p1 != NULL && p2 != NULL){
                    if(p1 == p2) return 1;
                    p1 = p1 → next;
                    p2 = (p2 → next != NULL)? P2 → next → next : NULL;
          }
          return 0;
}
function is called on the following linked list:

The value is returned by the code is:
solution:
Answer: 0

Explanation: The function implements Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm (tortoise and hare). It returns 1 if it detects a cycle, otherwise it returns 0.

  • Initial positions: the slower pointer starts at the second node (value 2) and the faster pointer starts at the third node (value 3) when the list has at least two nodes.

  • Movement: on each loop the slower pointer moves one step and the faster pointer moves two steps.

  • For the given list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → null, the faster pointer reaches the end (null) without ever meeting the slower pointer, so no cycle is found.

Therefore the function returns 0 (no cycle).

title: What does the following function do for given linked list
subject: Data Structure
text:
What does the following function do for a given linked list with first node as head?

void fun1(struct node* head)
{
        if (head == NULL)
                return;
        fun1(head->next);
        printf("%d", head->data);
}

options.html: Print all nodes of linked list in reverse order

solution:
Concept — in a recursive traversal the position of the work relative to the recursive call fixes the order in which nodes are processed. Work written before the call runs on the way down the structure, giving head-to-tail order; work written after the call runs while the call stack unwinds, giving tail-to-head order. The recursion still visits every node exactly once unless the advance step itself skips links.

Application — read the three lines of this function against that rule:

  1. if (head == NULL) return; is only a stopping rule. It ends the chain of calls at the end of the list and produces no output of its own.

  2. The advance step fun1(head->next) moves exactly one link per call, so every node of the list is reached and none is skipped.

  3. The output line printf("%d", head->data) is written after that call. The current node therefore contributes its value only once the entire remainder of the list has already contributed its own.

Cross-check — trace the list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. The calls descend to the end without printing anything, and the output is produced during the unwind:

Unwind step

Node being returned to

Output so far

1

5

5

2

4

5 4

3

3

5 4 3

4

2

5 4 3 2

5

1

5 4 3 2 1

Contrast — moving the output line above the recursive call would print 1 2 3 4 5 instead, and advancing by two links would drop every second node. Neither change is present here, so all five values appear and the order is the reverse of the list.

Result — the function prints the data of every node of the linked list, from the last node back to the first. For 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 the output is 5 4 3 2 1.

optionFeedback.html: This describes head-to-tail printing: every node contributes its data, and the value stored in the first node appears first in the output. Code that behaves this way places the print statement before the step that moves on to head->next, so each node is emitted on the way down the list.

This describes head-to-tail printing of every second node: the value stored in the first node appears first and one node in between is left out each time. Code that behaves this way advances two links at a time with head->next->next, or gates the print statement on a parity counter.

This describes tail-to-head printing: every node contributes its data, and the value stored in the last node appears first in the output. Code that behaves this way places the print statement after the step that moves on to head->next, so each node is emitted only once the rest of the list has been handled.

This describes tail-to-head printing of every second node: the value stored in the last node appears first and one node in between is left out each time. Code that behaves this way combines a two-link advance with a print statement placed after the traversal step.

title: The following function takes singly linked list as input argument.
subject: Data Structure
text:
The following C function takes a singly linked list as input argument. It prints its elements from the end using with the help of some other data structure. Some part of the code is left blank.
typedef struct node{
          int value;
          struct node next;
}node;
void printlist(node head){
          if(!head)return;
          ____________
}
Choose the correct alternative to replace the blank line:

options.html:
while(node != next){
printf(“%d”,head -> data);
printlist(head → next);}

solution:
Improved solution: Use recursion to traverse to the end of the list and print nodes while unwinding the recursion (the call stack acts like a temporary stack).

  • Base case: if head is NULL, return.

  • Recursive step: call the function on the next node to reach the list end first.

  • After the recursive call returns, print the current node's value so printing happens from last to first.

Minimal replacement lines (the exact lines to use in the blank):

printlist(head->next);

printf("%d", head->value);

Complete function example (including base case):

void printlist(node *head) {

if (!head) return;

printlist(head->next);

printf("%d", head->value);

}

Notes: ensure the node pointer field names match the struct definition (here shown as value and next) and use -> to access fields through a pointer.

optionFeedback.html: This prints the current node value before recursing, so it will output the list in forward order rather than from the end. Also the struct field shown is named value, not data; the intended approach is to recurse first and then print.

This is syntactically incorrect and conceptually wrong: it uses undefined identifiers (node and next) and a while loop structure that does not implement the required recursive reversal. The correct approach is to use recursion to reach the list end and then print on the way back.

Correct. Recursing first traverses to the end; when the recursive calls return, each node is printed, producing output from the last node to the first. Remember the base case if(!head) return; and use the actual field name (value) when printing: printlist(head->next); printf("%d", head->value);

"None of the above" is incorrect because a valid replacement exists: recursing into the next node and printing after the recursive call achieves printing from the end. The correct replacement is to call printlist(head->next) first and then printf the current node's value.

title: You are having pointer to the head of singly linked
subject: Data Structure
text: You are having a pointer to the head of singly linked list. The list either terminates at null pointer or it loops back to some previous location (not necessarily to the head of the list). What is the time complexity of best algorithm to find whether the list loops back or ends at a null location?

options.html: It is the time proportional to the length of the list
Algorithm exist but it finds only whether the list end with null point and loops infinitely if the pointer loops back to some previous location

solution:
Problem: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle or ends at null.

Floyd’s Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare) works as follows:

  1. Initialize two pointers at the head: slow moves one step at a time, fast moves two steps at a time.

  2. If the list has a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually meet the slow pointer inside the cycle.

  3. If the list ends at null, the fast pointer (or its next) will become null before any meeting occurs.

Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of nodes. Each pointer advances through the list at most a constant number of times relative to n.

Space Complexity: O(1) extra space using two pointers. As an alternative, you can detect a cycle by storing visited nodes in a hash set (O(n) time and O(n) space).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. There do exist algorithms to detect a cycle in a singly linked list. The standard Floyd’s cycle-finding algorithm (tortoise and hare) detects a loop in linear time O(n) using only O(1) extra space. Another approach uses a hash set to record visited nodes (O(n) time, O(n) space).

Correct. The fastest standard algorithm for detecting a cycle runs in linear time O(n). Floyd’s cycle-finding algorithm uses two pointers moving at different speeds: if there's a cycle they meet; otherwise the fast pointer reaches null. This approach uses O(1) extra space. An alternative is using a hash set to record visited nodes (also O(n) time but O(n) space).

Incorrect as stated. O(1) time is not achievable for this problem because you may need to examine all nodes to determine whether a cycle exists. You might be confusing time with space: cycle detection can be done in O(1) extra space (using two pointers), but the time complexity of the best algorithm is O(n).

Incorrect. The described behavior (algorithm that runs infinitely on a cyclic list) is not true for correct cycle-detection algorithms. Floyd’s algorithm terminates in both cases: if there is a cycle the two pointers meet (so the algorithm detects the cycle), and if there is no cycle the fast pointer reaches null. The algorithm does not loop forever on cyclic inputs.

title: Which of the following is true about linked list implementation
subject: Data Structure
text: Which of the following is true about linked list implementation of stack?

options.html: In push operation, if new nodes are inserted at the beginning of linked list, then in pop operation, nodes must be removed from end.
In push operation, if new nodes are inserted at the end, then in pop operation, nodes must be removed from the beginning.

Both of these are true: that if new nodes are inserted at the beginning in push operation, nodes must be removed from the end in pop operation; and that if new nodes are inserted at the end in push operation, nodes must be removed from the beginning in pop operation.

Neither of these is true: that if new nodes are inserted at the beginning in push operation, nodes must be removed from the end in pop operation; or that if new nodes are inserted at the end in push operation, nodes must be removed from the beginning in pop operation.

solution:
Key idea: To maintain Last In First Out (LIFO) order, push and pop must operate at the same end of the linked list — whichever end you insert at, you must also remove from.

  • Head-based stack: Insert new nodes at the beginning (head) and remove nodes from the beginning (head). This gives O(1) time for both push and pop on a singly linked list and is the simplest correct implementation.

  • Tail-based stack: Insert new nodes at the end (tail) and remove nodes from the end (tail). This also preserves LIFO, but on a singly linked list removing from the tail requires traversing the list (O(n)) unless you use a doubly linked list or maintain extra pointers.

Cross-check by elimination: A scheme that inserts at one end and removes from the opposite end always returns the node that has remained in the list the longest (the oldest surviving node) — that is FIFO (queue) behavior, not LIFO (stack) behavior. Both push-at-head/pop-at-tail and push-at-tail/pop-at-head are opposite-end schemes, so neither preserves LIFO; therefore the option asserting that both of these schemes hold is also not a valid description.

Conclusion: None of the three preceding statements correctly describe a linked-list stack implementation, since a valid implementation always pushes and pops at the same end.

optionFeedback.html: This option pairs pushing at the head with popping at the tail: since new nodes always enter at the head, the tail node is the one that has remained in the list the longest among those still present, and reaching the tail from the head pointer takes O(n) time on a singly linked list.

This option pairs pushing at the tail with popping at the head: since new nodes always enter at the tail, the head node is the one that has remained in the list the longest among those still present; removing the head is an O(1) operation on a singly linked list, though appending at the tail itself takes O(n) time without a maintained tail pointer.

This choice combines two separate claims about opposite-end schemes: inserting at the beginning while removing from the end, and inserting at the end while removing from the beginning. In each of these schemes, because new nodes always enter at only one end, the node removed from the opposite end is always the node that has remained in the list the longest among those still present — treating both claims as holding.

This choice combines the same two separate claims about opposite-end schemes: inserting at the beginning while removing from the end, and inserting at the end while removing from the beginning. In each of these schemes, because new nodes always enter at only one end, the node removed from the opposite end is always the node that has remained in the list the longest among those still present — treating neither claim as holding.

title: Polynomial addition is implemented using data structure.
subject: Data Structure
text: Polynomial addition is implemented using ______ data structure.
solution: A Linked List is the most efficient data structure for polynomial addition. Each node represents a term containing a coefficient, an exponent, and a pointer to the next term. It dynamically handles any number of non-zero terms sorted by exponent order without wasting contiguous memory space. The correct option is C.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Trees are hierarchical structures and are unnecessarily complex for linear operations like standard polynomial addition.
Incorrect. Stacks follow Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) access, which doesn't support the random alignment of terms based on matching exponents.
Correct! Singly linked lists naturally adapt to dynamic sizes, making it easy to insert, traverse, and merge sorted polynomial terms.।
Incorrect. Queues use First-In-First-Out (FIFO) access, which restricts the simultaneous tracking and computation of varying degree exponents.

title: The time complexity of searching an element in linked list
subject: Data Structure
text: The time complexity of searching an element in linked list of length n will be:
solution: To search for an element in a singly or doubly linked list of length n, you must traverse it sequentially starting from the head node. In the worst case (if the element is at the end or not present), you have to check all n nodes. Therefore, the time complexity is O(n). Thus, Option C is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. O(n log n) is typically the time complexity of efficient comparison-based sorting algorithms like Merge Sort or Quick Sort, not for searching a linear linked list.
Incorrect. O(log n) is the time complexity of Binary Search. Binary Search cannot be directly applied efficiently to a standard linked list because it lacks random/direct access to middle elements.

Correct. Since elements in a linked list are not stored in contiguous memory locations, sequential searching (Linear Search) is required. In the worst-case scenario, it takes n comparisons, which is O(n).

Incorrect. O(n^2) is the worst-case time complexity for simpler sorting algorithms like Bubble Sort or Insertion Sort, or nested loops. A single linear traversal for searching only takes linear time, O(n).

title: What is the time complexity to count the number of
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the time complexity to count the number of elements in the linked list ?
solution: Counting elements in a linked list requires traversing all nodes from head to tail. This linear traversal means time complexity is O(n) where n is the number of nodes.

optionFeedback.html: This option assumes constant time access like an array. However, linked lists lack random access. You must traverse each node sequentially to count them.
Correct. Counting elements requires single traversal O(n)
Counting elements requires single traversal O(n), not logarithmic time.
O(n²) represents quadratic time for nested loops. Counting requires single traversal, so check if you confused this with sorting or duplicate removal algorithms.

title: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion in singly
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion in a singly linked list?
solution:
A singly linked list node stores only its data and a pointer to the next node — there is no random-access index and no pointer back to the previous node. To insert a new node at any target position, you must therefore walk the list one hop at a time from the head until you reach the node just before that position; only once you are there does the actual relinking (creating the new node and updating two pointers) happen in constant time.

  1. Take a concrete singly linked list of n = 4 nodes: A (index 0) → B (index 1) → C (index 2) → D (index 3), where "→" denotes each node's next pointer.

  2. To insert a new node at index k, you must first reach the node currently at index k−1 (the predecessor) — because updating a node's next pointer requires already holding a reference to that node. Example: inserting a new node X at index 2 (so it lands between B and C) needs the predecessor at index 1, i.e. B, reached from the head A in k−1 = 1 hop (A → B).

  3. Once the predecessor is reached, the relink is O(1): set X's next pointer to the predecessor's current next node (X's next = C), then update the predecessor's next pointer to X (B's next = X). The list becomes A → B → X → C → D.

  4. This (k−1)-hop traversal is smallest when k = 0 (inserting at the very head needs no predecessor at all — the head reference is simply reassigned directly, 0 hops) and largest when k = n, i.e. appending after the current last node: for this same 4-node list, that predecessor is D at index 3, reached in n−1 = 3 hops (A → B → C → D).

  5. Since the question does not restrict where the insertion happens, the worst case is this k = n scenario: n−1 traversal hops before the O(1) relink. This scales linearly with n, giving O(n) overall.

Cross-check: this matches the general rule for singly linked lists — cost is governed by how far the target position is from the head, since there is no way to jump directly to an interior or trailing node the way an array’s index allows. Inserting exactly at the head (k = 0) is the one position that needs no traversal and runs in O(1); that is a special/best-case scenario for a specific position, not the answer to "what is the worst case across insertion in general". Considered over all valid insertion positions, the worst case is O(n).

So the worst-case time complexity of insertion in a singly linked list is O(n).

optionFeedback.html: O(1) describes a cost that stays the same no matter how large the input is — for example, accessing an array element by its index, or updating a pointer when the target location is already known.
O(log n) describes a cost that grows logarithmically with input size, as the relevant search space shrinks by a constant fraction each step — for example, binary search over a sorted array.
O(n) describes a cost that grows in direct proportion to the input size — for example, scanning every element of an unsorted array once, or summing all elements of a list.

This growth rate corresponds to nested iteration over the input — for example, comparing every pair of elements in a list, as a naive nested-loop duplicate check does; the cost grows with the square of the input size.

title: What is the main advantage of using linked lists compared
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the main advantage of using linked lists compared to arrays ?
solution: Arrays are stored in contiguous memory and provide O(1) random access by index, but resizing an array or inserting in the middle can require moving many elements. A linked list stores elements as separate nodes connected by links, so it can grow and shrink dynamically and insertions or deletions can be done by updating links when the position is known. Therefore, the main advantage of linked lists over arrays is dynamic size manipulation.

optionFeedback.html: Arrays provide faster random access because indexing an array element is O(1). Linked lists require traversal, so random access is slower, usually O(n).
Correct. Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically by changing links between nodes, and insertions or deletions do not require shifting all later elements as in arrays.
Linked lists usually require extra pointer handling and dynamic allocation, so memory management is not simpler than arrays.
There is a clear advantage among the options: linked lists support dynamic size manipulation more naturally than arrays.

title: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an element in an unsorted linked list ?
solution: To search for an element in an unsorted linked list, we must traverse the nodes sequentially from the head. Since the list is unsorted, there is no way to predict where a specific value might be located or skip any nodes. In the worst-case scenario, the target element is either at the very end of the list or not present at all. This requires visiting every single node in the sequence exactly once to confirm its absence or find it.",

optionFeedback.html: This option assumes constant time access like an array index. In a linked list, you must traverse nodes sequentially to find the target element.
Logarithmic time requires sorted data or binary search capabilities. Unsorted linked lists require linear traversal to locate any element.
This option correctly identifies the worst-case complexity as O(n).
This option suggests O(n2), which is incorrect for a simple linear search.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q158
subject: Data Structure
text: A linked list is preferred over arrays when
solution:
Concept: An array stores its elements in one contiguous block of memory, so every element sits at a fixed, computable offset from the start of the block. A linked list instead stores each element in its own separately-allocated node, connected only by a pointer to the next node, with no requirement that nodes sit next to each other in memory. This one structural difference is what makes each data structure cheap at different operations.

Application:

  1. Because array elements are contiguous, reading the element at position k is a single address computation (base address + k times element size), which takes constant time regardless of array size. But inserting or removing an element in the middle of an array forces every following element to be shifted over by one slot to keep the block contiguous, which takes time proportional to the number of elements that follow.

  2. Because linked-list nodes are connected only by pointers, inserting a new node right after a node you already have a reference to means creating the node and relinking two pointers — a fixed, constant amount of work no matter how long the list is. Deleting a node is likewise just bypassing it with a pointer update, with no other node touched.

  3. Applying this to the four listed conditions: repeated insertion and removal at various positions — the operation that is expensive for an array and cheap for a linked list — is exactly the condition under which a linked list is the preferred structure.

Cross-check — why the other conditions do not point to a linked list:

  • Fast indexing is needed: retrieving an element by position relies on a direct offset computation, which contiguous array storage supports in constant time; a linked list has no such offset and must be walked node by node from the head, so this condition does not call for a linked list.

  • Memory is static: a storage size that is fixed once and does not change is the array's allocation model; it describes upfront, unchanging memory, not a reason to favor a structure whose nodes are instead allocated one at a time as needed.

  • Elements are uniform: every element being the same type and size is what lets an array compute a single fixed per-element stride for its offset formula; it says nothing about how costly insertion or deletion is, so on its own it gives no reason to prefer a linked list.

Result: the condition that makes a linked list preferable over an array is frequent insertion and deletion.

title: Which statement accurately describes how to traverse singly linked list?

solution:
To traverse a singly linked list, you must start at the head node because it is the only entry point to the data structure. From there, you follow the 'next' pointer of each node sequentially to access the subsequent nodes in memory. This process continues until you encounter a null reference, which indicates that there are no more nodes in the list. This linear progression is fundamental to singly linked lists as they only store forward references.

Incorrect. Singly linked lists do not possess previous pointers. That is a distinguishing characteristic of a doubly linked list.

title: What does the following function do for given Linked List
subject: Data Structure
text:
What does the following function do for a given Linked List with first node as head?

void fun1(struct node* head)
{
    if (head == NULL)
        return;
    fun1(head->next);
    printf("%d ", head->data);
}

options.html: Prints all nodes of linked list in reverse order

solution:
Concept:

In a recursive function, whether a statement is written before or after the recursive call decides its execution order. Any statement BEFORE the recursive call runs in the same order the calls are made (head to tail). Any statement AFTER the recursive call runs only once that deeper call has returned — during the call stack's 'unwinding' phase — so those statements execute in the reverse of the call order.

Application:

  1. fun1(head=1) checks head != NULL, then immediately calls fun1(2) — node 1's printf has NOT run yet.

  2. fun1(2) similarly calls fun1(3) before its own printf runs.

  3. This continues through fun1(3) -> fun1(4) -> fun1(5) -> fun1(NULL).

  4. fun1(NULL) hits head == NULL and returns immediately — this is the base case, and no call has printed anything yet.

  5. Control now unwinds back up the stack: fun1(5) resumes and executes its printf, printing 5.

  6. fun1(4) resumes next and prints 4, then fun1(3) prints 3, fun1(2) prints 2, and finally fun1(1) prints 1.

  7. The full printed sequence is 5 4 3 2 1.

Cross-check:

Each recursive call advances by exactly one node (head->next), so every node in the list is visited exactly once — none skipped — ruling out both 'alternate node' options. And since each node's printf is deferred until its own call unwinds, the output order is exactly reversed relative to the list's head-to-tail order, matching the option describing reverse-order printing of ALL nodes.

optionFeedback.html: This option does not specify a print order, so it fits only if the values come out in the same head-to-tail order the list is given in. But the printf here runs AFTER the recursive call fun1(head->next), so a node's value is not output until every node ahead of it has already been processed — meaning the actual print order does not follow that straightforward head-to-tail sequence.

Since printf runs only after fun1(head->next) has fully returned, a node's value is output only once every node ahead of it has already been printed — for the list 1->2->3->4->5 this means 5 prints first, then 4, 3, 2, and 1 last, giving the output 5 4 3 2 1.

This assumes the recursive call skips a node, as if the code called fun1(head->next->next), so only every second node would be visited. The code instead calls fun1(head->next), advancing by exactly one node each time, so no node is ever skipped.

This carries the same skip assumption as alternate-node printing — it would require the recursive call to advance by head->next->next to bypass nodes, which the code does not do. The recursive call here always advances by exactly one node, so every node is visited.

title: What is the time complexity of the best-known algorithm for
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the tight asymptotic time complexity of the best-known algorithm that reverses a singly linked list in consecutive groups of size k? For example, 20 → 40 → 60 → 80 → 100 → 120 → 140 → 160 → NULL with k = 3 becomes 60 → 40 → 20 → 120 → 100 → 80 → 160 → 140 → NULL, where the final group may contain fewer than k nodes. Here, n is the number of nodes and n > 3.
solution:
CONCEPT: For a linked-list algorithm, total time is found by summing the work charged to all node visits. If each node undergoes only a constant number of pointer reads and writes, the total time is linear in the number of nodes, regardless of how those nodes are partitioned into groups.

APPLICATION: Apply that accounting to groups of size k.

  1. A complete group contains k nodes, and reversing it in place requires Θ(k) pointer operations.

  2. There are ⌊n/k⌋ complete groups, plus at most one final group containing fewer than k nodes.

  3. The complete groups therefore cost Θ(⌊n/k⌋ · k). If the remainder contains r nodes with 0 ≤ r < k, its cost is Θ(r), hence O(k). Their sum is Θ(n).

CROSS-CHECK: Charge each pointer update to the node being reversed. Every node is visited and relinked only a constant number of times, so the total charge is proportional to n.

RESULT: The best-known in-place group-reversal algorithm runs in O(n) time. An iterative implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space.

optionFeedback.html: This factorization models Θ(k) work charged separately to each node, as in a design with k distinct operations nested inside every node visit.
This factorization models Θ(log k) work charged to each node, as in a design that performs a balanced search or divide-and-conquer subroutine over k items per visit.
This factorization models an amortized constant amount of pointer work charged to each visited node during a complete traversal.
This factorization models Θ(n) work nested inside another n-scale loop, such as a full-list scan during each outer iteration.

title: Which of the following operations is performed more efficiently by
subject: Data Structure
text: Which of the following operations is performed more efficiently by doubly linked list than by linear linked list?

options.html: Deleting a node whose location is given
Searching an unsorted list for a given item
Inserting a node after the node with a given location
Traversing the list to process each node

solution:
Concept

The time for a linked-list update depends on which neighbouring nodes are already reachable. A singly linked node stores only a next link, whereas a doubly linked node stores both next and previous links.

When the target node itself is given, a backward link can remove the need to search for its predecessor; operations that already have the required node or must inspect every node gain no such asymptotic advantage.

Application

  1. Let x be the given node. Deleting x requires changing its predecessor’s next link so that it bypasses x.

  2. In a singly linked list, x does not identify its predecessor. Starting from the head to locate that predecessor takes O(n) time in the general case.

  3. In a doubly linked list, x.prev gives the predecessor directly. Updating x.prev.next and, when present, x.next.prev takes O(1) time.

  4. Therefore, deleting a node whose location is given is performed more efficiently by a doubly linked list.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Searching an unsorted list may inspect every node in either representation, so it is O(n) in both.

  • Inserting after a known node already has the splice point, so it is O(1) in both.

  • Traversing to process every node necessarily visits all nodes, so it is O(n) in both.

Result: deleting a node whose location is given is the operation with the asymptotic efficiency advantage.

optionFeedback.html: Deleting a known node reconnects the nodes immediately before and after it; the update uses the links adjacent to the target.
Searching an unsorted list compares each visited node with the target; the process follows successive links until a match or the list end.
Inserting after a known node reconnects that node to a new node and the new node to the former successor; the update starts at the given node.
Traversing the entire list processes each visited node in sequence; the process follows successive links until the list end.

title: Doubly linked list is declared as struct Node int Value;
subject: Data Structure
text:
A doubly linked list node is declared as shown below (illustrated in multiple languages for reference):

struct Node {
       int Value;
       struct Node *Fwd;
       struct Node *Bwd;
};

// Struct definition in C

    struct Node *Fwd;

// Struct definition in Java

    Node Fwd;

# Class definition in Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.Value = value
        self.Fwd = None
        self.Bwd = None

// Class definition in JavaScript
class Node {

        this.Fwd = null;
        this.Bwd = null;

}

Here, Fwd and Bwd represent the forward and backward links to the adjacent elements of the list. Let X be a pointer to a node in this list (declared in C/C++ style, as above) such that X points to neither the first nor the last node (that is, X refers to an interior/middle node). Which of the following C/C++ code segments correctly deletes the node that X points to, i.e. removes that node from the list while preserving the links between its neighbours? Evaluate each segment strictly under C/C++ pointer semantics.
solution:
Concept: To delete an interior node from a doubly linked list, you reconnect its two neighbours to each other so the node is bypassed — the node before it must have its forward pointer moved past it, and the node after it must have its backward pointer moved past it. This two-pointer reconnection works only when the node being removed has both a valid previous and a valid next neighbour, which the question guarantees for X.

Application: For node X with previous neighbour X->Bwd and next neighbour X->Fwd, deleting X requires exactly two pointer reassignments:

  1. Point the previous neighbour's forward pointer past X, to X's next node: X->Bwd->Fwd = X->Fwd;

  2. Point the next neighbour's backward pointer past X, to X's previous node: X->Fwd->Bwd = X->Bwd;

After these two assignments, X's former neighbours reference each other directly, so X is fully bypassed (and its memory can then be freed).

Cross-check: The remaining segments fail for two different reasons. Two of them use the '.' operator on a pointer expression (e.g. X.Fwd or X->Bwd.Fwd) — in C, member access through a pointer requires '->', so these segments do not even compile. The remaining segment uses valid '->' syntax but assigns each neighbour's pointer back to itself instead of to the sibling node, so the neighbours never end up linked to each other and X is not actually bypassed. Only the pointer-correct, logic-correct segment removes X while preserving the chain.

optionFeedback.html: This segment assigns to the previous node's forward-link field the current value of X's forward-link field, and assigns to the next node's backward-link field the current value of X's backward-link field.

This segment writes one assignment using the '.' operator directly on the pointer expression naming X's previous node, and a second assignment using '.' directly on the pointer X itself, in each case immediately followed by a field name.

This segment writes two assignments that use the '.' operator directly on the pointer X, and both right-hand sides are also expressed using '.' directly on X rather than on a distinct node reached through X.

This segment assigns to the previous node's forward-link field a value drawn from that same previous node itself, and assigns to the next node's backward-link field a value drawn from that same next node itself.

title: In the given elements doubly linked list to find 4th
subject: Data Structure
text: In a doubly linked list containing n elements, how much time will it take to find the 4th node from the end, assuming only a pointer to the head of the list is available?
solution:
Concept

For any query that must locate a node at a fixed offset from the end of a linked list, the achievable time complexity depends entirely on what reference the list already exposes. A singly-directional structure reachable only from a stored head reference gives no way to jump directly to a position counted from the end — you cannot skip nodes you have not yet visited — so any such query needs work proportional to the list's length. Only when a direct reference to the required end (e.g. a tail pointer) is already stored can the same query be answered in a small, fixed number of steps.

Application

Here only a head pointer is available (no tail pointer is stated), so the 4th node from the end must be located using one of the following, both proportional to n:

  1. Two-pointer technique: advance a lead pointer 4 nodes ahead of a follow pointer, then advance both one node at a time until the lead pointer reaches the end of the list — the follow pointer now sits at the 4th node from the end.

  2. Length-count technique: traverse once to count the total number of nodes, n, then traverse again from the head for (n - 4) steps to reach the same node.

Both methods visit each node only a bounded number of times (at most two full passes), so the time taken grows linearly with n.

Cross-check

If the list instead stored a direct pointer to the last node, the 4th-from-end node could be reached by moving back exactly three prev pointers from that tail reference — a fixed number of steps, independent of n. But the stem grants only a head pointer, so that shortcut is not available here, confirming that the time required scales with the size of the list rather than being constant.

optionFeedback.html: Quadratic time describes work that scales with the square of the list's size — the kind of cost seen if, for every node examined, the rest of the list had to be scanned again (for example, comparing every pair of nodes, or restarting a full traversal for each node considered). This task asks for one specific node defined by its position from the end; it does not involve comparing pairs of nodes or restarting a traversal for each node considered, so this growth pattern does not match what the task calls for.

With only a head pointer available (no direct reference to the last node), reaching a node measured from the end still requires visiting nodes in proportion to n. For example, using two pointers with a fixed 4-node offset between them — or first counting the list's length and then walking forward the appropriate number of steps from the head — each node is visited only a bounded number of times, so the work grows linearly with n.

This complexity class typically arises when a linear scan is combined with a logarithmic step, such as a divide-and-conquer approach, a sort-based method, or a lookup within a balanced structure. Locating a single fixed-position node in a linked list involves no dividing of the list, no sorting, and no balanced-structure lookup, so this level of complexity does not apply to this operation.

Constant time would require reaching the target node without the work depending on n at all — for instance, if the list already stored a direct reference to the node needed (such as the last node) and the target could be reached via a small, fixed number of hops from that stored reference. The stem does not state that such a direct reference is available here, so reaching a node measured from the end still depends on how far it is from wherever traversal begins, not on n being irrelevant.

title: Which of the following operation is performed more efficiently by

Time complexity summary:

  • Inserting after a given node: O(1) in both singly and doubly linked lists (when the insertion point is known).

In a singly linked list, if only the node to delete is given, you must traverse from the head to find its predecessor before you can remove it, which takes O(n) time.
Not more efficient. Searching an unsorted list requires examining nodes one by one in both singly and doubly linked lists, so the time complexity is O(n) in both cases.

Not more efficient. Inserting a node after a given node is O(1) in both singly and doubly linked lists when you already have a reference to the insertion point, because only a constant number of pointer updates are needed.

Not more efficient. Traversing the entire list to process each node visits every node once, so it is O(n) for both singly and doubly linked lists; the extra back pointers do not reduce full traversal time.

title: In circularly linked list organization, insertion of record involves the
subject: Data Structure
text: In a circularly linked list organization, insertion of a record involves the modification of
solution:
Concept — in a singly linked list every node carries exactly one link field, next, naming its successor. The chain a traversal follows is nothing but these link fields, so the shape of the list can be changed only by assigning a new target to some node’s next field. The cost of a structural operation is therefore the number of next fields it has to assign; reading a link costs nothing.

Application — insert a new node N into a circular singly linked list immediately after an existing node P, whose current successor is P.next:

  1. Locate P, the node after which N is to sit. Walking the ring to reach P only reads link fields, so nothing has been assigned yet.

  2. Assign N.next = P.next. The new node now names the same successor that P names, so everything that already followed P hangs behind N.

  3. Assign P.next = N. Now P names N, so N becomes reachable from the ring and the chain reads P, then N, then the node that used to follow P.

No other node has its link field touched. Because the list is circular there is also no NULL terminator to repair, since the ring closes through links that were never written. Exactly two link fields are assigned, so insertion modifies 2 pointers.

Cross-check — drop either assignment and the insertion fails, which is what makes both of them load-bearing:

  • Without N.next = P.next, node P names N but N’s own successor is still uninitialised, so a traversal that reaches N walks straight out of the ring.

  • Without P.next = N, node N names the right successor but nothing in the ring names N, so no traversal ever reaches it and the list is unchanged as seen from outside.

Contrast — counting link writes for the neighbouring operations makes the difference explicit.

Operation

Link fields assigned

Which ones

Search or traverse the ring

0

none, links are only read

Insert N after P

2

N.next, then P.next

Delete node C, which follows P

1

P.next alone

Reverse the whole list

one per node

every node’s next, driven by the working variables prev, curr, next

The deletion row is the one that is easy to carry over by mistake. When a node is removed, its own link field may be left stale because nothing reachable names it any more, so a single write keeps the ring correct. Insertion has no such shortcut: the node being added starts outside the ring, so both the link into it and the link out of it have to be written.

Result — insertion of a record in a circularly linked list modifies 2 pointers.

optionFeedback.html: Zero next-field writes. No node has its successor assigned, so no link in the ring points anywhere new; with nothing assigned, the ring that a traversal walks after the step is exactly the ring it walked before.

One next-field write. One node has its successor assigned, so one link in the ring points somewhere new; a single assignment redirects that node alone, and every other successor field keeps the target it already held.
Two next-field writes. Two nodes have their successors assigned, so two links in the ring point somewhere new; two assignments cover both of the link ends that meet at a single position in the ring.
Three next-field writes. Three nodes have their successors assigned, so three links in the ring point somewhere new; on a ring of three nodes, three assignments cover every link the ring has.

title: Which of the following is true for doubly linked list
subject: Data Structure
text: Which of the following is true for a doubly linked list compared to a singly linked list?

options.html: It uses more memory due to the additional pointer stored in each node.
It reduces the time complexity of every operation compared to a singly linked list.
It does not allow traversal in both directions.
It is faster to search for an element.

solution:
A singly linked list node stores only its data plus a pointer to the next node, so movement is possible in one direction only. A doubly linked list node adds a second pointer to the previous node. That single extra field per node is the entire structural difference between the two lists, and every comparison between them, memory, traversal direction, and which one operation gets faster, follows directly from it.

Checking each offered claim against that one difference:

  • Memory: a doubly linked list node always carries one more pointer field than a singly linked list node, so it always uses more memory per node, regardless of list length.

  • Time complexity: only operations that need a node's predecessor (deleting a given node, or inserting before it) get faster, because the previous pointer gives direct access instead of a scan from the head; traversal, inserting after a node, and searching for an arbitrary element remain asymptotically the same in both, so a blanket "every operation is more efficient" claim is false.

  • Both-direction traversal: the previous pointer lets you move backward from any node, so a doubly linked list explicitly supports both-direction traversal rather than lacking it.

  • Search speed: finding an arbitrary element still means scanning node by node from a start point in both structures, so the worst-case search cost is identical.

Re-deriving from the definition (doubly linked list = singly linked list + a reverse pointer) confirms only the memory claim holds unconditionally; the traversal-direction and search-speed claims are the opposite of true, and the time-complexity claim is true only for the narrow case of deleting an already-referenced node.

So the statement that is true for a doubly linked list compared to a singly linked list is: it uses more memory due to the additional pointer stored in each node.

optionFeedback.html: A doubly linked list node stores the data field plus two pointers (previous and next), while a singly linked list node stores the data field plus only one pointer (next). That extra previous-pointer field is present in every node, so a doubly linked list always consumes more memory per node than a singly linked list holding the same data, independent of list length or how it is traversed.

Not every operation becomes faster: traversal, inserting after a node you already hold, and searching for an arbitrary element all remain the same asymptotic time as a singly linked list. Only operations that need a node's predecessor, such as deleting that node or inserting something before it, improve, because the previous pointer gives direct access to the predecessor instead of a separate scan from the head; so "every operation" overstates this narrower benefit.

A doubly linked list node keeps a pointer to the previous node in addition to the next-node pointer, so from any node you can move forward or backward. Traversal in both directions is exactly the capability this structure adds over a singly linked list, not something it lacks.

Locating an arbitrary, unsorted element still requires scanning node by node from a starting point in both structures, so the worst-case number of nodes visited, and hence the search time, is the same for a singly linked list and a doubly linked list. Having a previous pointer does not let a search skip ahead or jump to the target.

title: Consider the following function, to which pointer to the root
subject: Data Structure
text:
Consider the following function, to which a pointer to the root node of the binary tree T is passed.

int KG(Struct Node *root)

{

int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0;

if(root == NULL) return 0;

if(root -> left == NULL && root -> right == NULL) return 1;

a = KG(root -> left);

b = KG(root -> right);

c = 1 + max(a, b);

return c;

}

The above program computes,

options.html: The number of edges in the longest path from root to leaf in T
The number of nodes in the longest path from root to leaf in T

solution:
Answer: This function returns the number of nodes in the longest path from the root to a leaf (the height of the tree measured in nodes).

Key reasoning:

  • Base cases: if root == NULL the function returns 0 (empty subtree height 0). If the node is a leaf (both children NULL) the function returns 1 (path of one node).

  • Recursive step: a = KG(root->left) and b = KG(root->right) compute the heights (in nodes) of the left and right subtrees. Then c = 1 + max(a, b) selects the larger subtree height and adds 1 for the current node, giving the longest root-to-leaf node count through this node.

  • Examples: single node -> returns 1; a chain of three nodes (root->child->grandchild) -> returns 3; a root with two leaf children -> returns 2.

Notes on related quantities:

  • Number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path: this equals the node-count result minus 1. For a single-node tree the number of edges is 0 while the function returns 1.

  • Total number of nodes in the tree: to compute that instead you would change the combine step to c = 1 + a + b (sum left and right subtree sizes plus current node) rather than using max.

  • Number of leaves: to count leaves you would return 1 for a leaf and otherwise return left_count + right_count (sum), not the maximum.

Conclusion: The code computes tree height measured in nodes (the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path), so the correct description is the number of nodes in the longest path from root to leaf.

For a single-node tree the function returns 1, whereas the number of edges on that path would be 0. To get the number of edges you would subtract 1 from the node-count result (or adjust the base case so a leaf contributes 0 instead of 1).

Correct. The function returns the number of nodes in the longest path from the root to a leaf (the tree height measured in nodes). It returns 1 for a leaf and for any node returns 1 plus the maximum of the heights of its subtrees, which yields the longest root-to-leaf node count.

title: If is binary tree with nodes, then the number of
subject: Data Structure
text: If T is a binary tree with N nodes, then the number of levels is at least:
solution:
A binary tree with L levels (root at level 1) is perfect when every level is completely filled; such a tree holds at most 2L − 1 nodes, since level i can hold at most 2i−1 nodes and summing from i = 1 to L gives 2L − 1. The number of levels needed for N nodes is therefore minimized only when the tree is packed as close to full as possible, and grows larger as the tree becomes more skewed.

  1. For a tree with L levels, the maximum node capacity is 2L − 1 (a perfect binary tree).

  2. To hold N nodes in L levels requires 2L − 1 ≥ N, i.e. 2L ≥ N + 1, i.e. L ≥ log₂(N + 1).

  3. Since L must be a whole number of levels, the smallest valid L is the ceiling of this bound: Lmin = ⌈log₂(N + 1)⌉.

Check with N = 4: ⌈log₂(5)⌉ = ⌈2.32⌉ = 3. A tree with 2 levels can hold at most 22 − 1 = 3 nodes, which is fewer than 4, so 2 levels are not enough; a tree with 3 levels can hold up to 23 − 1 = 7 nodes, which comfortably fits 4 — confirming that 3 is indeed the minimum.

So the minimum number of levels for a binary tree with N nodes is ⌈log₂(N + 1)⌉.

optionFeedback.html: ⌈log₂(N + 1)⌉ is the minimum number of levels because a perfect binary tree with L levels can hold at most 2ᴸ − 1 nodes; the smallest integer L for which 2ᴸ − 1 ≥ N is exactly the ceiling of log₂(N + 1).

N − 1 is the number of edges (equivalently, the height measured in edges) of a completely skewed binary tree — a single chain of N nodes. As a fixed expression in N, it never adjusts for how the tree is actually shaped — it always evaluates to N − 1, even though a more balanced tree of the same size needs far fewer levels than that.

N levels results only in the worst case, where the binary tree is a fully skewed chain and every node has at most one child; this is the maximum possible level count for N nodes, not a lower bound on it.

Flooring the value here yields the largest integer L for which 2ᴸ ≤ N + 1, which means 2ᴸ − 1 can still be less than N — a binary tree with that many levels may not have enough capacity to hold N nodes, so this expression can understate what is actually needed.

title: Which of the following statements about the following binary tree
subject: Data Structure
text:
Which of the following statements about the following binary tree is FALSE?

Text alternative: A is the root. Its children are B and C; B has children D and E; C has children F and G; D has children H and I; E has children J and K; and F has left child L.
solution:
Concept

A binary tree limits each node to at most two children. A binary search tree adds an ordering rule: every key in a left subtree is smaller than its ancestor key, and every key in a right subtree is larger. A complete binary tree fills every level before the last and places last-level nodes from left to right without gaps.

Application

  1. Read the root and its first child pair: A is the root and B is its left child.

  2. Apply BST ordering to that pair: a left child must be smaller than its parent, whereas B follows A alphabetically. Therefore the BST ordering rule is violated.

  3. Check completeness: levels containing A; B, C; and D, E, F, G are full, while H, I, J, K, L occupy the leftmost positions of the last level.

  4. Check the relations: J and K share the immediate parent E, and B lies on the path A → B → E → J.

Cross-check and contrast

  • “It is a binary search tree” conflicts with the ordering rule at A and B.

  • “It is a complete binary tree” agrees with the level-by-level left-filled layout.

  • “J and K are siblings” agrees with their shared parent E.

  • “B is an ancestor of J” agrees with the root-to-J path.

Result: the false statement is “It is a binary search tree.”

optionFeedback.html: For the claim “binary search tree,” the governing comparison is left-subtree key < ancestor key < right-subtree key. In the diagram, the root-left pair is A and B.
For the claim “complete binary tree,” inspect level occupancy from left to right. Levels 0–2 contain 1, 2, and 4 nodes, and the five nodes on the last level occupy its first five positions.
For the claim about J and K, siblinghood depends on sharing one immediate parent. The two parent links from J and K both terminate at E.
For the claim about B and J, ancestry is determined by the root-to-target path. The path to J is A → B → E → J.

title: What is the maximum number of nodes at level in
subject: Data Structure
text: What is the maximum number of nodes at level L in a binary tree, assuming the root is at level 0?
solution:
Concept: In a binary tree every node has at most two children. If levels are numbered starting from 0 at the root, a single root occupies level 0, and each level below can have at most twice as many nodes as the level directly above it, since every node passes on at most 2 children to the next level. This gives a doubling (geometric) relationship between a level’s index and its maximum node count.

Application: Building up level by level from the root:

  1. Level 0 (the root itself): at most 20 = 1 node.

  2. Level 1: each of the root’s up to 2 children gives at most 2 × 1 = 21 = 2 nodes.

  3. Level 2: each node at level 1 contributes at most 2 children, giving at most 2 × 2 = 22 = 4 nodes.

  4. In general, level i has at most twice the maximum of level i-1, i.e. 2i nodes — this follows by induction on i.

  5. Applying this to level L: the maximum number of nodes at level L is 2L.

Cross-check: Sum the per-level maximums for a perfect binary tree of height h (levels 0 through h): 20 + 21 + … + 2h = 2(h+1) - 1, which is exactly the well-known total-node-count formula for a perfect binary tree — confirming the per-level formula 2i is consistent.

Result: The maximum number of nodes at level L, with the root at level 0, is 2L.

Note: this question anchors the root explicitly at level 0 — the convention used by GATE-style/competitive DSA courses and most standard algorithms texts (e.g. CLRS). Some other textbooks number the root as level 1, under which the analogous maximum at level L would instead be 2(L-1); always confirm which convention a source uses before applying either formula.

optionFeedback.html: With the root fixed at level 0, level L holds at most 2L nodes: starting from the single root, each node contributes at most two children to the next level, so the maximum count doubles at every step down — the standard geometric growth of a binary tree.

This value matches the maximum count at level L only under a root-at-level-1 numbering scheme. This question’s stem explicitly fixes the root at level 0, a different convention — this option applies the wrong convention for the level numbering the stem specifies.

This expression totals every node from level 0 through level L-1 combined in a perfect binary tree — the cumulative sum across levels, not the capacity of one single level. Re-derive the count for level L alone, not the running total below it.

This formula happens to coincide with the true maximum at a couple of specific levels by coincidence; pick a level where it disagrees, such as L = 3, and the value differs from the actual maximum — squaring the level index is not, in general, the right relationship for a binary tree’s per-level node capacity.

title: Which of the following is NOT type of binary tree

text: Which of the following is NOT a type of binary tree ?
solution: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, referred to as the left and right child. Common classifications include complete binary trees, where all levels are fully filled except possibly the last; full binary trees, where every node has either zero or two children; and balanced binary trees, which maintain height balance for efficient operations. Therefore, among the given options, a circular binary tree is the only one that does not exist as a standard classification within computer science data structures.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - December 2009 - source Q21
subject: Data Structure
text: If the number of leaves in a strictly binary tree is an odd number, then what can you say with full conviction about total number of nodes in the tree ?

options.html: It cannot be equal to the number of leaves.
It is always greater than twice the number of leaves.

solution:
Concept

A strictly binary tree (a full binary tree) is one in which every node has exactly 0 or 2 children. If L is the number of leaf nodes (0 children) and I is the number of internal nodes (exactly 2 children), the identity L = I + 1 always holds for such trees, and the total node count is N = L + I.

Application

  1. From L = I + 1, we get I = L − 1.

  2. Total nodes: N = L + I = L + (L − 1) = 2L − 1.

  3. The stem gives L as odd. Substituting into N = 2L − 1: 2L is always even (2 times any integer), so N = (even number) − 1 is always odd.

  4. So whenever L is odd, N = 2L − 1 is guaranteed to be odd.

Cross-check

Take a concrete strictly binary tree with L = 3 leaves (odd). Then I = L − 1 = 2 internal nodes, so N = 5, an odd number — matching the derivation. A minimal case also checks out: a single-node tree has L = 1 leaf (odd), I = 0, N = 1, also odd.

This also rules out the other statements: since N = 2L − 1 is strictly less than 2L, N can never exceed twice the leaf count. Since N = 1 = L when L = 1, N can equal the leaf count in at least one valid strictly binary tree. And since N = 2L − 1 is always odd, N is never even.

Result

The total number of nodes in the tree is always an odd number.

optionFeedback.html: This option characterizes the total node count N as odd — that is, N leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2 (N = 2k + 1 for some integer k).
This option characterizes the total node count N as even — that is, N leaves no remainder when divided by 2 (N = 2k for some integer k).
This option characterizes a relationship in which the total node count N never equals the leaf count L, for any strictly binary tree of any size.
This option characterizes a relationship in which the total node count N always exceeds twice the leaf count, i.e., N > 2L, for every strictly binary tree.

title: The in-order traversal of tree resulted in FBGADCE. Then the
subject: Data Structure
text: The in-order traversal of a tree resulted in FBGADCE. Then the pre-order traversal of that tree would result in
solution:
Concept

A binary tree is uniquely reconstructable only when an inorder traversal is paired with a preorder (or postorder) traversal: inorder fixes the left-right ordering, while preorder/postorder fixes which node is the root at each level. Inorder ALONE does not determine a unique tree, so in principle several different preorder strings can match one inorder string.

To make such a problem well-posed, the standard convention (and the one the ISRO key uses) is to assume a complete / balanced binary tree, built by recursively choosing the MIDDLE element of each inorder segment as that segment's root.

Application

Apply the middle-as-root rule to the inorder string FBGADCE:

  1. Whole segment FBGADCE -> middle element A becomes the root; everything left of A (FBG) is the left subtree, everything right of A (DCE) is the right subtree.

  2. Left segment FBG -> middle element B is its root, with F as B's left child and G as B's right child.

  3. Right segment DCE -> middle element C is its root, with D as C's left child and E as C's right child.

Now read this tree in preorder (root, then left subtree, then right subtree): A, then the left subtree B F G, then the right subtree C D E.

Preorder result: ABFGCDE.

Cross-check

Read the constructed tree back in inorder (left, root, right): left subtree gives F B G, then root A, then right subtree gives D C E -> FBGADCE, which matches the given inorder exactly. So the complete-tree reconstruction is consistent.

Note on the reported ambiguity: because only the inorder was supplied, AFGBDEC is also a mathematically valid preorder for FBGADCE (it corresponds to a different, skewed tree). The exam, however, fixes the intended tree with the complete/balanced convention above, and the official ISRO 2011 key is ABFGCDE. The solution therefore states ABFGCDE as the accepted answer while acknowledging that the bare inorder, on its own, is not enough to force a single tree.

optionFeedback.html: Try to use FGBDECA as the preorder together with the given inorder FBGADCE: at the very first split the letters that must fall into the left part and the right part do not match the counts the inorder demands, so the subtrees cannot be filled consistently. FGBDECA is therefore not a valid preorder for this inorder at all.

ABFGCDE matches the tree obtained by taking the middle element of each inorder segment as its root (A over the segment, then B over FBG and C over DCE). Reading that tree root-first, left, then right yields exactly this string, and reading it left-root-right reproduces the given inorder FBGADCE.

If FBGADCE is the inorder and BFGCDEA is taken as the preorder, the partition it forces at the top assigns the wrong number of letters to one side, so the remaining letters can no longer build matching left and right subtrees. BFGCDEA does not satisfy the inorder/preorder consistency check, so it is not a valid reconstruction.

AFGBDEC is genuinely one of the preorders that the inorder FBGADCE can produce, which is why this question is sometimes called ambiguous. The ISRO 2011 key, however, fixes a single intended reconstruction of the tree, and AFGBDEC is not the one that key selects, so it is not the accepted answer for this question.

title: Generate binary tree for following table and find the height
subject: Data Structure
